Three-dimensional random close packing (RPC) of numerous objects is a widespread phenomenon observed in numerous fields, spanning from engineering to biology. Despite extensive study, no comprehensive explanation has been developed for three-dimensional random close packing (RPC) until now. Our research delves into the properties of hard spheres during packing and finds a phase change from an unfrustrated to a frustrated phase in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional random close packing when the packing density exceeds a certain threshold. We predictively identify two new polar crystalline phases displaying frustration at a higher density, marked as FPC2-D and FPC3-D, where one negative eigenvalue appears in the phonon spectrum. Our study also uncovers additional phase transitions among these phases when the packing density changes. To explain these phase transitions, we utilize a geometrically based theory, extending the Pashley-Abrham descriptor. Our research provides insights into various phenomena associated with three-dimensional random close packing, including changes in viscosity, relaxation time, and changes in phonon properties. Our findings provide a basis for understanding the dynamic and thermal behavior of densely packed hard-sphere systems.

Pretrained language models have demonstrated impressive performance across various downstream tasks. A crucial aspect of these models is the introduction of specially designed tokens, which are processed differently from standard tokens, to aid in handling specific tasks. Nonetheless, over-reliance on these extra tokens often results in subpar performance in uncomplicated tasks or those without explicit labeling. To address this limitation, we have developed an approach to detect and eliminate unnecessary special tokens to prevent contamination of the embedding space. As a result, this method enables the removal of overfitting special tokens to specific tasks and improves the overall robustness of the pretrained models, as evidenced by our experiments conducted on tasks such as aspect sentiment analysis and abstractive sentiment summarization. Furthermore, our results indicate that our proposed method outperforms or complements existing state-of-the-art techniques for removing extra tokens.

A novel evaluation metric for tracking network changes has been proposed, based on the classic problem of evaluating additions to a set. This metric has been applied in various theoretical contexts, including logic, Combinatorial mathematics, and graph theory, where it has also served as a starting point for more in-depth analysis. To gauge the effectiveness of different network theories, this metric is used to compare the performance of page-ranking algorithms, notably, PinS and PageRank, which are used to evaluate the quality of network additions in various contexts, such as network expansion, synthesis, and clustering. The proposed method involves modeling PageRank as a distribution over network edges and comparing it to PinS, which is handled differently. The results indicate that PinS outperforms PinS in nearly all the benchmark datasets generated, across all the different dataset characteristics studied, significantly outperforming it by 52%, across these benchmarks.

Using molecular dynamics simulations, we investigate the global link between space and time variability in a mixture of glass-forming substances, specifically propylene carbonate, across its thermodynamic range. We discover and verify a scaling rule, based on thermodynamic entropy change, that governs how the system changes over time across its entire thermodynamic spectrum. This rule is linked to the changes in entropy and how energy levels spread out, providing insight into the system's dynamics and how it changes over time.

The observed scaling rule applies broadly, even to moments of the system that are normally rare, describing how energy levels spread out. Breaking down the system into its individual parts and studying their behavior allows us to understand the patterns of movement and relaxation within the system. The application of the Frenkel-Kontorova Hamiltonian helps us understand how constraints affect the system's dynamics, while the presence of disorder leads to the loss of crystal-like behavior and the emergence of additional time scales.

In addition, we explore how the system's dynamics changes when it is cooled down, observing the emergence of additional time variability, reversing the standard ordering of time variability, and the temporary presence of variability connections. These observations support the idea that time variability is an independent physical property, separate from the system's thermodynamic properties and state of order.

Recent studies indicate that transformer models are susceptible to errors caused by negation sensitivity. We build on existing research by examining how various categories of negation affect the natural language inference task using modern transformer models as benchmarks. Our investigation covers six diverse categories of negation and NLI datasets developed by Liu et al. Our key findings reveal that certain categories of negation noticeably impair the performance of SOTA models, particularly absolute and moral negations. Furthermore, we discover that data augmentation and model scaling can mitigate the negation sensitivity issue to some extent. Our research provides an in-depth analysis of the underlying causes and potential solutions to this negation sensitivity problem.

We propose a look-ahead attention mechanism to anticipate distant influential tokens in neural machine translation. The LookAheadAT mechanism is integrated into the standard Transformer encoder, allowing it to consider the future relevance of tokens in addition to contextual importance. By doing so, it improves the model's ability to capture long-range connections. We test various LAt implementation designs and demonstrate that it can enhance translation quality using existing translation datasets. Notably, it performs particularly well in scenarios with significant long-range dependencies, such as translating technical news from Chinese to English.

Our research focuses on the geometry of cotangent bundles within the context of weighted Riemann surfaces. When the total space of a complex line bundle is equipped with a Hermitian metric and a connection, its fiber as a one-dimensional submanifold inherits a similar structure. However, the curvature of this induced metric, typically a diagonal element, is typically zero when the line bundle is holomorphic. Conversely, if the total space is a symplectic manifold, this curvature becomes non-zero and takes the form of a triholomorphic curve. By drawing from Weyl's classical work on cotangent bundles, our analysis extends the expression of these curvature weights to their complete forms, going beyond prior studies that relied on flat connections and avoiding "Weyl's trick" that relies on a flat metric. Additionally, our results also apply to the Laplace operator on one-forms with a modified connection thatincorporates the symplectic form, and have implications for the Fourier transform of parabolic equations related to the Dolbeault Laplacian.

The boundary Casimir effect is examined through the lens of holography in scenarios where a boundary is warmed from outside. In three-dimensional space-time, it is discovered that the underlying boundary field theory's thermal entropy and internal connections between fields are unaffected. In contrast, in a five-dimensional space-time, it is found that the radiation and energy linked to the boundary are influenced by the field theory's internal connections. Using Wick rotation and black hole computations, these results are verified and extended to higher-dimensional cases. These findings are in line with predictions based on an entanglement point of view.

This research presents an innovative approach to computing the partial derivatives of the Asian option pricing function with respect to the volatility of the underlying asset, focusing on reduced memory requirements. Building on Wu's [1] formula that expresses the single Laplace transform of the Asian option pricing function of a geometric Brownian motion in terms of the European option pricing function, our approach further leverages the partial value decomposition property to efficiently handle multiple Laplace transforms. Consequently, our method requires only the computation of a European option pricing function and its partial derivative for initial conditions, while enabling the rapid calculation of multiple partial derivatives with minimal memory usage.

Recent data from the Fermi-LAT telescope indicates that nearly half of the Earth's diffuse gamma-ray background is attributed to galaxy clusters. To further investigate this, we aimed to determine the contribution of galaxy clusters as a whole to the extragalactic gamma-ray background. To this end, we turned to the Fermi-LAT catalog, which currently identifies over 3,800 galaxy clusters. Employing a simplified model, we calculated the expected gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters and compared it to actual observations. Notably, we found that the combined gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters aligns with data from the Fermi-LAT, suggesting that they indeed play a major role in shaping the extragalactic gamma-ray background. Moreover, our analysis shows that earlier estimates overestimated the gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters by a factor of three, leading to excessive predictions. Consequently, this revision brings the predictions into line with data and eliminates the need for additional gamma-ray sources to explain the background, thereby simplifying our understanding.

Inflation models with sharp features in their potential or sound horizons leave distinct signatures in primordial non-Gaussianities, which can be modeled using a perturbed equation of state. This phenomenon allows for the detection of features in the power spectrum and bispectrum, even with limited signal-to-noise ratio. The bispectrum parameter $\beta$ correlates with the coefficient of the sharp feature in the equation of state and can be accurately constrained using the two-point correlation function and microphysics for features beyond the horizon. However, features within the horizon are difficult to constrain through the bispectrum. This regime is particularly sensitive to variations in the equation of state and can be probed through the cross-correlation of the temperature and polarization maps, potentially revealing features in the inflationary potential that are masked by Planck data.

We have developed the Latent Visual Semantic Explainer (LaViSE), a method that creates natural language descriptions of a convolutional neural network's learned representations. LaViSE employs the SiPEAR dataset to capture the network's latent states and map them to textual descriptions through two distinct approaches: token-based replacement and neural machine translation. To improve these representations, LaViSE incorporates a neural optimizer, refining the Learned Representations to better describe the SiPEAR labels. During the optimization process, LaViSE generates descriptions for the refined representations, applying the generator to a validation set, thereby evaluating the effectiveness of the learned representations. LaViSE utilizes the sipear dataset and SiPEAR labels to achieve this purpose. We have successfully applied LaViSE to the sipear dataset, significantly increasing our understanding of the sipear dataset, particularly in terms of the sipear labels. LaViSE generates accurate and natural language descriptions for the sipear dataset, significantly increasing our understanding of the sipear labels. We have compared LaViSE with the LViSE and LViSE++ approaches, demonstrating that LaViSE surpasses its predecessors. We have also compared LaViSE with the state-of-the-art text-to-text transfer models, notably the T5 and BERT models, LaViSE outperforms these models.

Inspired by the increasing interest in one-dimensional (1D) materials with high-temperature superconductivity, we draw a parallel between the physical properties of a supersymmetric two-dimensional cuprate model and its one-dimensional counterpart based on the Luttinger tunneling mechanism. We then develop a theory that bridges the gap between these two models, highlighting the substantial overlap between their physical phenomena and thus solidifying the credibility of 1D superconductivity at high temperatures. Utilizing a generalized bosonization approach, we derive a conductance formula for a one-dimensional system with a finite length. Our prediction that a quantum channel opens up at low temperatures aligns with recent experiments on an unconventional superconductor known as Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer. Furthermore, we investigate superconductivity in systems with strong interactions and provide insights into unusual features observed in tunneling experiments using carbon nanotubes and tunneling spectroscopy using materials called InAs/InAs.

People living with HIV who are aware of the cost and wait times to access local clinics may be more likely to pursue treatment. To study the impact of treatment probability on the cost and travel time to access healthcare, researchers used a dataset from a South African study, estimating a discrete choice model based on a random effects formulation. The analysis revealed significant correlations between the cost and travel time of accessing healthcare, but the results did not establish a causal link between these factors and the likelihood of treatment, due to unobserved variables. However, researchers did demonstrate that reducing travel time to HIV clinics may increase the likelihood of treatment, regardless of the specific implementation approach. An additional causal analysis focusing on changes to the cost and travel time of accessing healthcare revealed that shorter travel times to HIV clinics, familiarity with travel times, and reduced waiting times for care may increase the likelihood of treatment, while reduced appointment costs may decrease it. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of travel costs and wait times to HIV clinics for treatment likelihood, but also emphasize the need for further research to better understand the underlying factors driving treatment behavior.

We have studied the transformation of a stable skyrmion lattice into a helical phase of magnets in a type of magnetic material, specifically the Ir$_{20}$Fe$_{80}$ ferromagnetic alloy. Our research used the internal field function of the Heisenberg model and applied the cluster perturbation theory to examine the effects of temperature and magnetic field on the skyrmion lattice. We found that the stable skyrmion lattice transforms into a helical phase when exposed to negative magnetic fields and that this transition is facilitated by the creation of domain walls. In contrast, the same transition in the metastable skyrmion lattice is driven by the thermally induced migration of magnetic domains. Our calculations also showed that the skyrmion lattice and helical phase have identical free energies but differ in their response to temperature and magnetic field. Finally, our research demonstrated that the transformation of the stable skyrmion lattice into the helical phase is a second-order phase transition characterized by divergent fluctuations.

We introduce a novel class of singular ARMA models that expand upon traditional ARMA models, incorporating specific factor-based structures that can be linked to high-dimensional dynamic factor models. A two-part estimation strategy, combining maximum likelihood and principal component analysis, is developed to efficiently handle the models as single, unified factors. Our theoretical generalizations ensure consistent estimation in large systems, backed by extensive simulation results. Additionally, we utilize the models to gain insights into the behavior of global financial markets, offering novel interpretations of the 2007-2009 financial crisis and correlations among market indices.

The primary objective of this research is to delve into the set of stationary points of the Moreau proximal mapping and demonstrate its equivalence, under specified assumptions, to the solution set of an equilibrium problem, particularly when it involves proximally regular problems. Furthermore, we establish that, when certain conditions are met, the solution set of an equilibrium problem corresponds to the stationary points of the squared distance function resulting from the Moreau proximal mapping. Additionally, we show that, in the event of monotonicity, the solution set of an equilibrium problem is also the fixed point set of the Moreau proximal mapping. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the concept of stationary points. Moreover, we introduce an algorithm designed to locate any point within the set of stationary points, rather than necessarily identifying the optimal solution.

It is widely acknowledged that overconfident predictive models can be improved by incorporating Bayesian methods to quantify uncertainty.  However, in deep learning, the implementation of Bayesian methods is often restricted due to the availability of suitable priors and the computational expense of sampling. In an attempt to address these issues, we propose an innovative approach to instill Bayesian principles into deep neural networks. The method involves combining two sampling-based techniques. The first technique uses Markov Chain Monte Carlo to update network weights in conjunction with a shrinkage-based data augmentation method. The second technique employs Monte Carlo expectation propagation to generate posterior distributions of layer outputs. The method allows for the propagation of uncertainty across multiple test inputs, and as such, yields a probabilistic output that is capable of quantifying uncertainty in computer vision tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation. The method has been successfully tested on various datasets, including CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Stanford Cars, with results revealing a noticeable reduction in uncertainty for out-of-distribution data.

Direct numerical simulations of dynamos in complex astrophysical objects like the sun and stars require comprehensive consideration of turbulent influences. Since realistic models are difficult to resolve in detail, researchers typically employ various forms of dynamical simplification. A recent study presented an approach for fitting compact magnetic field models to those that can be directly resolved, which was initially tested in turbulent flows without magnetic fields. In this work, we extend that method to scenarios with magnetic fields and find that it accurately represents the general magnetic field structure, except in areas where current simplifications apply, such as shock waves. We examine here three types of turbulent magnetic fields: those in different states of turbulence, and those with and without magnetic fields. We find that our model accurately predicts the overall magnetic energy, its distribution by scale, and the associated fluctuations in space and time. It effectively predicts the large-scale magnetic field structure, which results from dynamical forces, and the self-similar distribution of magnetic energy at smaller scales. We use this model to generate synthetic magnetic field configurations for larger-scale simulations, which lack the detailed resolution of smaller scales, and find it suitable for various astrophysical models.

Using new ALMA-12m CO(10)--$1$ unbiased molecular line surveys toward the strongly gas-dominated nucleus of NGC4945, we have made some key discoveries. The high-resolution maps reveal that the molecular outflow in this area has a 5 sigma detection of $5.9\pm1.8\times10^{8}$\Msol, representing about 7\% of the total gas outflow in this region. The mass outflow rate in this area is significantly higher compared to similar regions in other galaxies, such as NGC512, NGC1068, and Circinus. The velocity maps of the $^{12}$CO($1--0$) show that the gas outflow in this area has a velocity range of about $-600\sim-1200$\kms. The gas outflow in this area has also been detected through other molecules, such as CI($3--2$), CI($5--4$), and HCN($1--0$)). The velocity maps of these molecules reveal that they share similar velocity ranges with the $^{12}$CO($1--0$) maps. The gas outflow in this area has also been detected through CI($3--2$) and CI($5--4$) lines, showing that the gas outflow in this area has a velocity range of about $-600\sim-1200$\kms. In the context of quasilinear theory for weak turbulence, the evolution of two-electron distributions is examined. It is demonstrated that the rate of increase in wave spectral energy directly corresponds to the rate of change in the electron distribution's relevant quantity under the Vlasov-Maxwell system. Furthermore, specific particle probability density functions are derived for distinct wave types, including long-waved magnetosound, short-waved magnetohydrodynamic kinetic Alfvén waves, and long-waved whistlers.

We now offer in the widely-used SGLMs class the possibility to use an adaptive method for calculating the step size. The standard SGLMs were originally developed with a fixed step size, but by incorporating a technique for adjusting the step size, we can create a method that remains independent of the location of the solution's extremum. Unlike methods with an adjustable step size that only consider the local maximum or minimum of an function, our new approach can accommodate non-uniform data sets and still guarantees that the estimates remain unbiased. The performance of our new method was evaluated by comparing it with other techniques, such as the maximum likelihood and non-parametric approaches, on artificial and real data sets. The results show that it offers a good balance between efficiency and computational cost, but is not always the most efficient option.

Given a sectorial operator A generated by a C0-semigroup S, we examine a two-parameter Lyapunov inequality in the complex plane. It's demonstrated that solutions to this inequality result in boundedness of A's resolvent, while parameters within a specific sector ensure the C0-semigroup's left invertibility. This characterizes the "optimal" region in the complex plane containing the Lyapunov set, yielding specific conditions on contour integrals involving the resolvent that form the basis of a C0-semigroup's left inverse. We also discuss how these findings relate to well-posedness of parabolic PDEs with complex coefficients.

This study introduces MuMuPy, a software tool capable of simulating how dimuonium absorbs radiation and makes other key transitions, also calculating associated probabilities to high precision. Based on these predictions, it uses Bayesian networks to optimize the measurement of various fundamental constants involving the dimuonium spectrum. Additionally, it examines the possibility of detecting new physics at advanced levels of measurement. The research incorporates a user-friendly interface for easy calculation and visualization. Developed under an open-source framework, MuMuPy's code is freely accessible online.

We consider a portfolio optimization problem, in which an investor endeavors to maximize the long-term growth rate of their wealth, incorporating the notion of absolute and relative wealth in the utility function. By shifting focus to the relative wealth, we ensure the utility function is non-decreasing, and two distinct maximum likelihood equations are derived, one based on the absolute and the other on the relative wealth. By solving these equations, we obtain two candidate portfolios, which we find to be identical when the absolute wealth candidate is substituted into the relative wealth equation. Additionally, both portfolios align with previous optimal utility-maximizing investment strategies, namely the Constant Absolute Wealth and Constant Relative Wealth rules. Furthermore, by solving a differential equation derived from the relative wealth candidate, we find that it precisely follows a counting process under continuous time investment scenarios.

Young, luminous galaxies in the early Universe display properties similar to those of local Green Pea galaxies but with greater rest-frame far-ultraviolet brightness. To compare galaxy growth between these two groups, we used the GALEV code to run simulations of star formation and gas expulsion based on observed Green Pea galaxy data. We found that the resulting cluster luminosity functions match observed data, including both local Green Pea galaxies and young, luminous galaxies in the early Universe. By replicating the brightness of young, distant galaxies using the code, we found that it produces consistent results, indicating similar levels of star formation and a consistent mass range for the galaxies in question.

This research explores the behavior of fermions interacting with bosons in a pseudo-spin context, taking into account the effects of both temperature and an external magnetic field. The model can be applied to systems of fermions coupled to pseudo-spin, such as superconductors with Josephson junctions, superfluid He-3, and superconductors, among others. To investigate its properties, we utilize the functional density matrix approach, supplemented by the Popov approximation for bosons. Our results reveal an intriguing phenomenon where fermions exist in two distinct states, resembling both conventional quasiparticles and non-conventional quasiparticles associated with pairs of fermions. The later state is particularly well-suited for modeling superconductors. Building on these findings, we develop a comprehensive set of equations that incorporate the effects of temperature, external field, and fermion-boson interaction, ultimately shedding light on the complex phase transitions encountered by fermions in these systems.

The braided Thompson's groups, building on the idea of braided spaces, were introduced in a 2020 paper. These groups naturally incorporate a braided space structure in their construction. In this work, we add to the existing definition of linear divergence for braided spaces and apply it to the braided Thompson's groups. We confirm that these groups exhibit linear divergence and also prove that their braided spaces structure is irreducible. Additionally, we demonstrate that the braided spaces structure in the original Thompson's group $V$ does not meet the criteria for being a braided Hopf space, addressing a previously unanswered question.

This paper presents an French RAG model pre-trained using the Google PaLM
approach, incorporating a combination of news and open source code datasets.
We demonstrate the effectiveness of this model in handling both by-task and
cross-task adaptations, fine-tuning it for diverse applications such as
automatic summarization, question answering, and other tasks, addressing key
challenges in handling long sequences and multi-task learning. Notably, the
model outperforms individual components in both adaptive reading comprehension
and automatic summarization benchmarks. Furthermore, when compared to RAG baseline
models, it achieves a significant 8.8 F1 score improvement in cross-task
adaptation accuracy.

Classical analysis and partial differential equations researchers utilize RH methods to analyze asymptotic, which also helps in understanding soliton dynamics. Building on this concept, I introduce an approach called "analysis by MHM" to discuss asymptotic behaviors by transforming analysis to meromorphic function behavior on a Riemann surface. This method involves three steps: meromorphic function representation, construction of an RH problem, and application of the IHM theorem. This strategy provides a new perspective to study asymptotic behaviors and expands the scope of RH methods. To illustrate the method's capabilities, we present three examples: microlocal projectors, T-RH problem solutions, and oscillating integrals.

To produce reliable annotations, specialized qualification processes are necessary 
for tasks that are still being developed, such as automatic summarization. This 
paper proposes the SummSum dataset, a collection of annotated summaries alongside 
unannotated ones from publicly accessible websites, enriched with expert-curated 
guidelines. This dataset serves as a resource for summarization researchers and 
solicits contributions from summarization practitioners to facilitate high-quality 
training datasets generation.

For text-video retrieval tasks, effectively capturing a video's combined spatial and temporal features is crucial. Recent studies have shown that a single model can efficiently perform video understanding, but current approaches typically rely on combining diverse, feature-dependent transformers with separate transformation capabilities, which may lead to complex decision-making and require extensive training data. In response, we introduce TS2-Net, a unique approach incorporating two type-II multi-head transformer variants that enable simultaneous spatial and temporal feature transformation. The first variant processes early features, grouping them by frame, and the second analyzes late features, grouping them by semantic object category. This allows TS2-Net to efficiently perform video understanding, even when trained on minimal data. Evaluations on MS COCO Visual Search and ActivityNet show significant improvements over current state-of-the-art models, with further analysis revealing TS2-Net's unique architecture yields stable performance even when heavily pruned or trained with reduced data.

A novel method for analyzing rare decays of the top quark at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has the potential to uncover early signs of new physics in complex Higgs models. By examining unique particle pathways and utilizing advanced event filtering techniques, researchers can increase sensitivity to anomalous effects by at least 50% compared to traditional methods, particularly in scenarios involving long-range particle interactions. Additionally, enhanced sensitivity can be achieved through the enhancement of signal pathways mediated by top quark pairs.

In real life, many networks are a combination of different types. In a new study, researchers create a random hybrid network by uniting two smaller networks grown through a preferential attachment process. When a new node enters the combined network, it connects to an existing node in a randomly chosen group, unlike in a typical preferential attachment network, where the new node chooses its connections randomly. In- and out-degree distributions, clustering coefficient patterns, and overall connectivity characteristics of this hybrid network are studied and compared to those of a pure preferential attachment network. Surplus degree over which in- and out-degree distributions start to differ was discovered and degree variance for both in- and out-degrees was found, showing hybrid networks diverge from purely preferential attachment networks. However, in- and out-degrees variance Hyperbolic distribution was found in a new range, expanding understanding of this distribution.

In the context of the Internet of Things (IoT), the problem of distinguishing wanted signals from unwanted interference is becoming increasingly critical. Most research in signal identification has focused on scenarios where the same communication technology is used for wanted and unwanted signals, yielding high accuracy rates. In contrast, cross-technology scenarios, which involve diverse communication technologies such as LoRa, WiFi, or NFC, result in signal misclassification rates ranging from 30% to as high as 90%. Consequently, determining whether interference is unwanted is highly significant. This paper introduces a novel deep neural network strategy called C4 or C Categorizer for four. The model is trained on a large dataset containing 104 categories of unwanted interference and can achieve an accuracy of nearly 80% when classifying same-technology interference, which is also the best recorded result to date. Additionally, a method called CrossCat utilizes the learned features from individual technologies to categorize cross-technology interference, demonstrating an accuracy of around 50%, a rate significantly higher than existing methods.

This work focuses on examining the dynamics of a complex Klein-Gordon particle (KG-particle) in three distinct spacetime contexts: de Sitter space, anti-de Sitter space, and spherically symmetric Einstein-Rosen spacetime. In each of these settings, we analyze how gravitational influence impacts KG-particles, and we explore the potential for spontaneous emission and decay. Additionally, we investigate the dynamics of these particles in a region where the gravitational field is absent. Our approach involves establishing a complete set of interactions between a massless scalar field and a massive KG-particle within a black hole background, and we examine the mass dependence of their resonant frequencies under the influence of gravity.

It's well-known that every countable locally standard measure algebra can be represented by a real number $\alpha$, specifically $\alpha\geq\alpha_{\mathfrak{c}}$, and this representation is unique up to equivalence. However, the question of whether there exists an $\alpha$ in this range with the property that the corresponding measure algebra has a $\mathbb{Q}$-basis has been disputed. This paper affirmatively answers this query, demonstrating the existence of an $\alpha$ in this range with the stated property.

The twist-3 parton distribution, known as the generalized parton distribution E, is difficult to measure in fixed target experiments because it cannot be determined from inclusive cross-sections due to undetermined integrals. A significant contribution to this ambiguity can be understood through a theoretical model called the "pompy" model, which is based on pomeron physics and represents a virtual exchange of reggeons and pomeron through a diagram. We explore how to extract information about twist-3 distribution, by examining how the pompy model affects a recent semi-inclusive sum rule and testing its applicability with target and single spin sum rule methods. We also analyze how model parameters can be set under certain conditions and assess their impact on calculating the twist-3 distribution from pompy diagram contributions. Furthermore, we evaluate the model's potential influence on detecting twist-4 effects.

Our work addresses two primary queries. Initially, we investigate whether linear classifiers can accurately learn and utilize complex, non-linear patterns in data, particularly in situations involving error correction. Furthermore, we aim to identify a general approach for linear classifiers to effectively counteract adversarial attacks, encompassing various forms of data manipulation. By developing a framework that measures a classifier's dependence on input data, we demonstrate that certain linear classifiers can indeed capture intricate, non-linear data correlations. Moreover, our research reveals that linear classifiers capable of correcting errors in high-dimensional systems must also be adversarially robust. Consequently, our approach can serve as a practical and efficient solution for safeguarding such classifiers against adversarial attacks, applicable to various forms of data manipulation. Notably, our findings validate the effectiveness of recent methods proposed to enhance the robustness of complex AI systems, even in cases involving limited training data.

To analyze many-body solitons in the presence of spin-orbit coupling and inter-species interactions between two bosons, we employ an analytical method. By converting the lattice system into momentum space and removing the complex Ginzburg-Landau phase, we investigate the solitons' properties. It is found that the spin-orbit coupling and inter-specie interactions lead to the emergence of superfluid phases, including ferromagnetic, spin-superfluid, and chiral superfluids, which are characterized by their unique properties. Moreover, we discuss possible experimental realizations of these solitons in Bose-Hubbard models.

This passage outlines a representation of finite abelian $p_r$-groups through a sequence of saturated Young diagram chains, based on a generalized version of Garsia's formula. The representation builds on a connection established in a preceding study, where a relationship between the $p_r$-part of Young tableaux's combinatorial properties and the $p_r$-structure of Young diagrams was established. The formula derived in this research will serve as the foundation for developing specific results.

Surface and line defects within diverse dimensions can be translated into simple expressions through the AdS/CFT correspondence, and in turn, these expressions provide unified explanations for the thermodynamic properties of horizons associated with these defects. Specifically, surface defects correspond to submanifolds within a spacetime, and line defects correspond to partially compactified dimensions. Our analysis focuses on three-dimensional black holes, magnetic monopoles, and surface defects, as well as line defects within five-dimensional gauge theories, including the Nambu-Segal-Bondi solution, black holes, magnetic monopoles, string sources, and a specific string tension model. By applying the Poincaré patch, delta-function sources, and specific tension models, we are able to derive these solutions from a unified perspective. Furthermore, we calculate the free energy, and in turn, the temperature and specific heat of these configurations, and find that they exhibit either Hawking or Bondi Accretion phenomena. Our analysis also extends to the black string tension model, and reveals that its free energy diverges as the string stretches, and in turn, undergoes tachyonic instability.

A novel method of visualizing and understanding kernel functions is introduced, 
representing them as trees (kernel trees). Kernel trees can be learned directly 
from data, serving as powerful features for data analysis and universal 
approximations. By utilizing these tree representations, kernel functions' 
properties are more easily interpreted. As an example, the method has been 
applied to understanding the structure of a kernel function derived from the 
Gaussian Process regression model. By utilizing this tree representation, the 
kernel functions' complexity is measured as the number of tree nodes, and its 
performance is evaluated through prediction accuracy. Experimental results 
demonstrate that kernel trees outperform Gaussian Process models on synthetic 
data sets. Furthermore, kernel trees have been successfully used to model complex 
data in a recent study.

A key consideration for muon collider design is minimizing the effect of in-flight muon decays in the accelerator. This requirement poses significant technical challenges for surviving such decays in detectors and poses further difficulties in accurately recording the decay products. This paper explores innovative design strategies for detectors that can mitigate the effects of in-flight decays and outlines specialized features necessary to handle decays in operation. The study primarily focuses on design requirements for a large-volume detector system capable of functioning effectively in the decay chain, with an underlying assumption that a muon collimator is used to reject in-flight decays. Several design concepts for the long muon decay chain are presented, with an emphasis on operational designs at 1.5 TeV and 4 TeV muon colliders.

A new approach called Spartan is introduced to create sparse neural networks by balancing the exploration of representation space against exploiting suboptimal models. During training, a neural network and its potential variants are simultaneously updated, where the exploration is driven by optimistically estimating the best possible performance of the most advanced variants, while the actual performance of the variants is used to exploit simpler representations and prevent overfitting. When combined with a technique that limits model complexity, Spartan particularly shows improved results in developing very sparse networks, surpassing the performance of state-of-the-art methods that initially appeared more efficient. Spartan particularly shows strong performance on ImageNet53 and ResNet120, demonstrating equivalent or superior performance compared to fully dense models while using significantly fewer parameters.

We're examining a 3D crossover between a Bose-Einstein condensate and a quark-gluon plasma that incorporates Pauli blocking. Our model involves the Dirac equation with a potential that varies across space and time, taking into account both bosonic and fermionic excitations, along with electromagnetic interactions. In the bose-bose scattering, we apply a cubic mean-field correction, leading to an approximate equation of state that incorporates both Pauli blocking and a bose-einstein condensate. In a 3D transition, bose-einstein condensation emerges from fermionic excitations through a process of back reaction. Initially, we examine a non-magnetic bose-bose scattering crossover, followed by a bose-fermion scattering crossover, where we consider distinct bose-fermion interactions, incorporating both Pauli blocking and a bose-einstein condensate. In a bose-fermion scattering crossover, various patterns of correlation and phase shifts emerge, influenced by bose-einstein condensates, Pauli blocking, and backflow effects. Finally, we compare our findings with an approach that does not consider Pauli blocking, revealing notable differences in phase shifts, densities, and energy densities at different stages of crossover, particularly in density ratios and ratios of densities to rest masses, leading to distinct values of net-mass ratios for bose and fermions.

To understand how developers view test smells, we conducted an exploratory study, gathering data through a survey answered by 17 developers who participate in a study programme focused on open-source software, including the etextbook and Django projects.  The participants were asked about their views on two specific test smells, namely, Red Green Refactor and Flaky Tests, using multiple-choice and open-response questions.  The choices for the multiple-choice questions were based on pre-existing studies, while the open-response questions aimed to gather additional insights into the perceived impact of test smells on project maintainability and potential suggestions for improving test smell detection and prevention mechanisms.  The analysis of the open-response data revealed that the developers slightly preferred the severity of Flaky Tests to reflect reality better, and we present some further insights into the views of these developers on test smells.

This study examines a non-monotone integro-differential process where a moving boundary function $\mathcal{Y}(t,\cdot)$ is defined as the solution to a differential inclusion $\mathcal{F}(t,\mathcal{Y}(t,\cdot))$. We show that an external process $x(t)$ with initial value $x_0$ within the domain $\mathcal{D}$ of $\mathcal{Y}(t,\cdot)$ follows a continuous solution path when it satisfies the differential equation $x(t) = f(t,x(t))$ for all $t \in [0,T]$ with initial condition $x_0 \in \mathcal{D}(0)$. We also establish that the solution map $S$ which takes initial values $x_0$ to final values $x(T)$ with respect to the topology induced by $\mathcal{D}$ is upper semicontinuous. Furthermore, this study also explores the existence of the solution for the control problem $x^{\mathpzc{c}}(t) = f(t,x^{\mathpzc{c}}(t)) + \mathpzc{c}(t)$ with initial value $x^{\mathpzc{c}}(0) = x_0$ within the domain $\mathcal{D}(t)$ for all $t$ within the time frame $[0,T]$.

The Monte Carlo event generator KKMCee, designed for muon and tau pair production, has been enhanced with several key upgrades. These advancements include a more precise treatment of radiation effects using the two-loop electroweak formalism and the inclusion of quantum corrections involving heavy flavor. A newly developed matrix element based on the \textsc{MadGraph} framework adds an extra level of accuracy. The improved algorithm also features faster convergence and reduced memory usage, allowing it to process events up to three times faster than its previous version. The results from analytical and numerical corrections are also compared to identify areas for further improvement.

Conventional energy-based methods for inter-beat interval extraction are hindered by the ECG's low energy in the 1 Hz range, particularly with noisy signals. Deep learning approaches can enhance IBI extraction, but they are heavily influenced by pre-processing methods. A novel deep learning technique has been developed to directly retrieve 1 Hz components from ECG signals, thus improving IBI extraction accuracy. This new approach also features a data augmentation method that allows for beat-to-beat independence in retrieval, further benefiting IBI extraction. Experimental results demonstrate the efficacy of this new approach, particularly in challenging environments, such as noisy conditions and heart rates nearing the vascular limits.

In the field of distributed computing, a novel randomized algorithm is developed to determine the singular value decomposition (sVD) of a data tensor, specifically the symmetric form known as t-SVD. This algorithm reduces the number of necessary data tensor passes to $O(k/\epsilon)$, significantly outperforming previous state-of-the-art approaches. Additionally, efficient computation of high-frequency t-SVD components is achieved by utilizing a specialized sample compression technique. This process involves data compression followed by a distributed application of the coarsened sVD, likely obtained from a lower-dimensional tensor evaluation. This allows for efficient computation of the first $k$ sVDs of the t-SVD. Both the compressed subproblem and the overall algorithm are rigorously analyzed, with a guarantee that the true sVD will never be approximated by a zero vector. This distinct guarantee, paired with the proven efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithm, make it a valuable tool for tensor signal processing applications.

Static graph embedding into low-dimensional Euclidean spaces has seen significant advancement, but the inclusion of changing edges presents an even greater obstacle. Real-world networks often exhibit this dynamic characteristic, making it crucial to develop methods for managing the perturbations in such networks. This work addresses the challenge of creating embeddings for dynamic graphs that account for the evolution of their structure. To achieve this, we propose an approach called D-LEA, which utilizes local geometric constraints to minimize disturbances and ensure that the resulting embedding accurately reflects the network's topology. This D-LEA embedding serves as a versatile tool, allowing for the management of varying perturbations and providing insights into the complex relationship between distance and time. Its applications extend to issues like quantifying node similarity, determining community affiliations, and making predictions, as it offers a scale of distances. Moreover, it provides a straightforward interpretation of nodes, making it an attractive solution. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in many aspects.

Our recent calculations using the resonant formalism of the Green's function within the continuum framework have involved studying the effects of meson nuclei clustering. The method has been applied to meson-nucleon scattering and decay processes of meson nuclei, with particular focus on the low-energy resonance characteristics of delta and lambda hypernuclei. The calculations have revealed the presence of a narrow low-energy resonance in $^7$H, in contrast to our previous findings. Additionally, for $^5_\Lambda$H, a bound state was observed at energies near the $\Lambda$n scattering threshold, accompanied by a narrow low-energy resonance. The second-order pole energy, $\varepsilon_2$, in $^5_\Lambda$H is significantly larger than the binding energy, explaining why the narrow resonance was not captured in our previous calculations.

In 1989, Gidas and Spruck investigated a Nirenberg type problem on half-spheres, obtaining a uniform bound for critical solutions. Building upon this, we have demonstrated a bound exists for supersymmetric variations, which, along with variational calculations, indicates a mountain pass level exists. Furthermore, we have observed a discrepancy between half-sphere and full-sphere problems; specifically, for half-spheres, solutions do not concentrate at one singular point; rather, they spread along the axis invariant under the $SO(2)$ group.

While effective, large-scale person re-identification often requires costly global memory storage and complex data management. Our solution circumvents these issues by leveraging the benefits of both class-centered and identity-based methods. A new deep class-wise discrepancy loss is introduced to refine the discriminative embedding space, leading to accelerated learning and reduced dependencies on initial random assignments. Our approach achieves comparable accuracy using a smaller model and reduces storage needs by half, outperforming current minimal-memory re-identification systems. The proposed technique demonstrates a 40.8% decrease in training time compared to the current benchmark and our model achieves a remarkable mAP of 78.54% on the large-scale ImageNet-VID dataset, surpassing the previous state-of-the-art. The code and model can be found on the repository at https://github.com/yichau/Deep-Me.

The English Test and Trace programme, implemented to combat the COVID-19 pandemic, encompassed local tracing partnerships as a key component. These partnerships, consisting of local authorities, private sector companies, and community groups, worked to bolster the Test and Trace effort by covering areas not reached by national contact tracers. Through a survey and case study analysis of nine local tracing partnerships, this research assesses their efficacy, considering factors such as contact rates, the speed of tracing, and the quality of services provided. The study reveals mixed outcomes, as some partnerships excelled in these areas, whereas others fell short. Notably, partnerships that established strong relationships with their local communities generally performed well. The speed of tracing operations also significantly impacted overall performance. Based on the findings, this research offers guidance and recommendations to enhance the performance of local tracing partnerships, emphasizing the importance of specific strategies to boost contact rates and the effective deployment of workforce resources.

Our analysis of Melotte 72, an open cluster located in the Galactic bulge, is 
based on two-field photometry covering approximately 17 arcminutes. With the 
help of Gaia EDR3 data, we have restricted our focus to 341 member candidates, 
selected through color-magnitude diagram and spatial location proximity. Our 
results indicate that Melotte 72 is approximately 872 million years old, with 
a total luminosity of -4.87, and an estimated mass of 10,000-20,000 M_sun. This 
makes Melotte 72 one of the oldest star clusters known, aged around 880 million 
years, placing it second in age after BH 48, an 890 million year old cluster. Our 
results are consistent with other age determinations based on Gaia EDR3 data but 
different from those generated from near-infrared data. Furthermore, we have 
observed an integrated U-band and V-band color of -4.87 mag and -5.67 mag, along 
with an extinction value of 3.51 mag. Melotte 72 is also found to have a mass 
function that follows a power-law distribution typical of young star clusters, 
and is characterized by a slope value of -1.8.

The large excursion behavior of simple stochastic processes, such as simple random walks and finite differenced Laplacian processes, is analyzed over three-dimensional Euclidean space. From these analyses, a phase transition occurs at a specific excursion level where the finite-volume process' properties transition into those of the underlying continuous random field. Subsequently, the two-dimensional case is examined, and a phase transition is discovered at a unique excursion level of random field excursions.

We introduce a new approach to camera calibration by leveraging direct regression, a method that outperforms traditional techniques such as Levenberg-Marquardt in our experiments. Based on the principles of differentiable optimization, direct regression can be integrated into either parametric or non-parametric camera calibration models, and we demonstrate its effectiveness using both methods. Our results showcase the superiority of direct regression in calibration accuracy, computational efficiency, and stability, particularly when applied to non-parametric calibration, where it can determine all camera calibration parameters at once.

Our research delves into the concept of constraints in the context of reinforcement learning, particularly from a regulatory perspective. We propose that an agent capable of adhering to constraints can utilize this knowledge in two relevant applications: adapting its existing policies or transferring its capabilities to new tasks. Our framework for modeling constraints is versatile, allowing it to be applied to a range of learning techniques. Our findings demonstrate the potential for policies optimized with the help of constraints to be more efficient in unfamiliar situations compared to those optimized without constraints. Additionally, constrained agents are more adept at adapting to new tasks where the existing actions remain relevant. However, when the circumstances change dramatically, a constrained agent may struggle to adapt, unlike agents optimized without constraints for specific environments.

The GAIA space mission, a flagship project of the European Space Agency, is a pivotal component of its Five-Year Plan and has far-reaching significance across multiple scientific domains. By observing the sky in different colors and measuring the positions and movements of approximately one billion celestial objects, GAIA allows scientists to reconstruct the galaxy and understand its dynamics better. This extensive 3D dataset contains detailed information on numerous celestial objects, including stars, galaxies, and black holes, providing a wealth of information and posing significant data analysis and scientific challenges. In the context of Gaia Data Release 3, researchers utilized advanced methods to analyze the red clump stars in the galaxy and create accurate maps of the galactic bulge and bar, while also conducting further studies on the galaxy's dynamic properties and the nature of dark matter. Furthermore, GAIA's observations have significant implications for the study of nearby galaxies and allow scientists to analyze the movement of dwarf galaxies and galaxy clusters, offering a unique understanding of the galaxy's complex evolution over time.

Our developed model, TreeLS, is an adaptation of the traditional Learning Augmented Decision Tree algorithm, integrated into an indexed tree structure.  TreeLS combines tree decomposition techniques with the benefits of Local Computation Algorithms, by solving classical graph problems like Vertex Cover and MaxCut on large graphs that are difficult to evaluate directly.  Instead, the graph's metrics and key properties are broken down into a tree of smaller components, allowing for efficient computation of critical attributes essential for making informed decisions.  Our experiments demonstrate that TreeLS achieves up to a 10-times speedup compared to the conventional approach, and accurately predicts approximately 90% of the remaining classification labels without fully evaluating the graph.

The continuous clustering coefficient has its roots in the standard universal clustering coefficient for undirected graphs and is designed to address its limitations. Unlike the standard clustering coefficient, which only evaluates a graph's clustering quality when it is completely connected or completely disjoint, the continuous clustering coefficient measures the similarity of a graph's clustering pattern to that of a completely connected graph. However, a graph's clustering pattern can be complex and difficult to analyze, which prompts the development of two new versions of the continuous clustering coefficient. One version simplifies the analysis by mapping a graph's clustering pattern to a binary code and then calculating the similarity, while the other version uses a key property of clustering patterns to define a more comprehensive and intuitive index. Unlike the standard clustering coefficient, which often produces false positives and fails to detect real-world networks, the continuous clustering coefficients reveal the distinguishability of real-world networks and random networks. Furthermore, the proposed indices are versatile and can be used to evaluate various types of networks, which is illustrated by its successful application to a Twitter network.

Certifying the predictive accuracy of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)
is vital due to their rising usage in various applications. Although,
formally validating PINN predictions against measurements is often
difficult, recent research has linked the method to bothistein and tikhonov regularizations,
enabling a posteriori error estimation. The underlying theory explains why
PINN error estimation works and how it relates to more traditional regularization
methods. It's also demonstrated that the method has practical limitations, including
the necessity to adjust the training process in order to obtain an accurate error
evaluation. The study further explores the theoretical connection between PINNs and
more traditional regularization techniques like Galerkin methods.

Spatial coverage models have been successfully applied across multiple disciplines, 
air pollution modeling being a crucial area of study. Spatial interpolation techniques 
are frequently used to determine short-term exposure levels. Since the characteristics 
of exposure paths show autocorrelation, researchers have employed models like the 
independent data transformation cover (IDTC) to create pseudo-independent datasets, 
allowing the application of machine learning algorithms. However, traditional evaluation 
metrics are lacking in precision as they do not account for exposure level disparities. 
We introduce a novel assessment framework that accurately measures the similarity 
between predicted and actual exposure level profiles. The proposed approach can 
be utilized to effectively evaluate the performance of any spatial air pollution model.

The bulk electronic transport of topological insulators is analyzed using a specific device setup that isolates only the edge currents of the two-dimensional helical topological insulator system. A notable zero-energy peak resulting from non-Majorana House effects at zero temperature is observed, but it significantly decreases with rising temperature. This reduction occurs due to the increased zero-energy peak width caused by the finite-temperature, standard Drude-like behavior is recovered at higher temperatures. Moreover, it was found that the device setup can function as a thermometer due to the temperature dependence of the zero-energy peak.

This study examines the spectral characteristics of linear bandit models and their implications for model choice and clustering. We establish the spectral properties of popular linear bandit models, develop sharp bounds on the spectral norms of certain matrices in Thompson sampling, and analyze their spectral behaviors. Our findings yield model selection and clustering strategies that are adaptive to unknown dimensions. We also compare the spectral characteristics of straightforward and efficient Thompson sampling algorithms. In a simulated environment, the proposed methods demonstrate comparable performance to information-theoretically optimal approaches but are more resilient to arbitrary data contamination.

Building on the success of the valley Hall effect, researchers have proposed an orbital Hall effect, claiming it offers a more direct way to measure a 2-dimensional material's conductivity. However, the orbital Hall effect is typically used to explain the anomalous Hall response, a property that is both inelastic and non-equilibrium-driven. Given that inelastic and non-equilibrium-driven responses are non-linear, it is difficult to distinguish between the orbital and valley Hall effects. Moreover, the anomalous Hall response can be separated into contributions from the valley and orbital effects, complicating the measurement. Consequently, the promise of the orbital Hall effect to provide clearer insight into conductivity remains uncertain until the distinct contributions of the orbital and valley effects can be isolated.

Adversarial Machine Learning problems can be effectively tackled using Reinforcement Learning (RL) methods, which offer an alternative to direct gradient optimization. While some approaches rely on simulated environments to balance privacy and performance, we present adversarial attacks trained through RL in real-world scenarios without requiring a balanced trade-off. Our attacks, trained in a self-play setting to learn against evolving defenses, demonstrate robustness across diverse settings and demonstrate our proposed algorithm's capability in a CGI image compression scenario. These findings indicate that RL-based adversarial training yields more stable and consistent outcomes than conventional methods.

In problem-ratio space, we propose a solution to source matching that leverages high-resolution space images. Our method combines top-ranked matches from image feature mapping with Bayesian score-ratios derived from image features, resulting in improved robustness and generalization compared to solely using image features. Furthermore, we introduce additional metrics based on photometric information, significantly enhancing the precision of source matching and surpassing state-of-the-art performance, with the precision increasing by 8% to 13% when this information is incorporated.

Given sets of cardinals, the task is to determine when the combination of cardinals resulting from the sum, product, or other operations, exceeds any given ordinal.  A set of cardinals is 'dominant' at an ordinal if this condition is met; it's 'cofinal' if there's at least one cardinal, the sum of which exceeds that ordinal; and it's 'nowhere stationary' if no proper subset fulfills this condition.  A set of cardinals is'satisfying' for an ordinal if the minimum possible size of such a subset meeting the dominance condition is exceeded only by that ordinal; and 'robust' if the removal of no element results in the satisfaction of the condition being met.  A key question, posed by D. Donder, concerns the existence of sets of cardinals, the sum of which exceeds all countable ordinals, but the sum of no proper subset does.  Our findings include that robust sets meeting these criteria exist; and, relatedly, the robustness of certain sets determines key properties they possess.

Ontology visualizations have become essential for understanding complex semantic networks. Although available visualizers can convey structural information, they struggle to represent conceptual content. We introduce OntoPlot, a tool designed to effectively visualize ontologies by seamlessly incorporating and aligning concept and instance data. Its user-friendly interface allows subject matter experts to efficiently create and explore study ontologies, thereby facilitating in-depth analysis and knowledge gain. Compared to alternative tools, OntoPlot excels in addressing numerous challenges, thereby providing a superior user experience. Through case studies and user feedback, we demonstrate OntoPlot's capabilities and showcase its potential in enhancing domain expert collaborations.

Our proposed CycleGAN-based approach aims to alleviate the issue of drift in deep feature representation across various modalities by utilizing CycleGAN-based training for both direct and indirect synthesis. Unlike traditional methods that perform single-domain-to-domain image conversion, our approach allows for bi-directional synthesis, ensuring that bi-directional conversions maintain original feature characteristics. By using CycleGAN, we effectively prevent the 'washout' effect, thereby preserving original input features in synthesized outputs. Additionally, our approach leverages domain-specific losses to maintain target domain features in synthesized outputs. Through applications to two challenging healthcare applications - autonomous breast cancer screening and colorectal polyp detection - our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in producing high-quality synthetic images for unseen modalities, reducing the need for expensive and hard-to-acquire data.

Deep generative models can create realistic data by learning various underlying factors that contribute to the generation of sensory data. Deep neural generative models have made significant advancements in understanding the intricate nature of unprocessed data such as images and videos, which are essential for our perception of the world. Conversely, our traditional understanding of the world is often rooted in a more fundamental aspect, namely the physical laws that govern the behavior of fundamental particles and forces. However, generating data through simulation poses a different challenge, one that demands greater precision and control compared to data obtained from sensory input. Furthermore, numerous data analysis and machine learning techniques are still limited due to the scarcity of simulated data. Our proposed method aims to address these issues by leveraging deep generative models to create realistic and detailed synthetic data. This would facilitate the filling of knowledge gaps resulting from incomplete simulations, as well as enable the enhancement of data-driven techniques with greater precision and control.

The ratio of the combined mass diffusion and heat transfer rates in a mixture undergoing temperature changes can be calculated using a generalized version of the Stefan theory. This calculation relies on the fact that the flexibility of the molecules in the mixture does not depend on the direction. When an equilibrium state is compared to a non-equilibrium state where there is a significant temperature difference, the variation in flexibility leads to a non-zero thermal diffusion factor. The thermal diffusion factor is directly related to the average change in the angle between adjacent molecules in the mixture. The rotation of the molecules in the mixture's presence of a temperature gradient corresponds to a non-spherical potential energy surface. This is particularly true for a mixture of carbon dioxide and carbon disulfide, where the intermolecular forces are anisotropic in nature. The thermal diffusion factor was found to be greater for carbon dioxide than carbon disulfide, with both diffusion processes being influenced by the flexibility of the molecules to varying degrees. The carbon disulfide showed a thermal diffusion factor close to zero due to its spherical potential energy surface. A combination of molecular dynamics simulations and experimental measurements revealed the thermal diffusion factor for carbon dioxide was 0.79, with an associated error of 0.03. A non-equilibrium molecular area per molecule instead of the mean squared radius of gyro around 29.5 square Angstroms was found to be well correlated with the thermal diffusion factor for carbon dioxide. A thermal diffusion factor for carbon dioxide of 0.78 was

In a field dominated by the transformers model architecture, we explore the potential benefits of adapting pre-trained language models for a specific task: human-level essay scoring. Our investigation involves an in-depth analysis of two approaches: fine-tuning these models with a relatively small number of parameters, and incorporating them into a multi-task learning framework. We demonstrate that by enhancing traditional transformers architecture with a novel component, such as the dynamic connection block, we can achieve performance comparable to larger, more complex models like the Unified Transformer. Our results also show that by incorporating a module like the dynamic connection block, we can reduce the number of parameters required to achieve state-of-the-art performance in our field, thereby facilitating applications such as automated grading systems.

Most deep neural network-based information retrieval systems are trained with
large amounts of labelled data. However, in many real-world scenarios, we often
lack labelled data but have access to a highly accurate, but time-consuming
search engine. We present a novel method to apply deep neural networks to
problem-solving without labelled data. Firstly, we reframe a false positive
suppression challenge into a box re-ranking problem using a strong, but time-
consumming search engine as a reference. We pre-train a deep neural network
using a siamese approach, taking unlabelled data as input. We assess the
neural network's performance using a temporal consistency approach, as its
performance directly translates to improved search results when used in combination
with the time-consuming search engine. We demonstrate the success of our
proposed model on two real-world datasets and show that it achieves results
comparable to a system trained with labelled data. We also highlight a
significant time-saving advantage. The proposed model's ability to learn without
labelled data makes it highly practical for use in real-world, labour-intensive
scenarios.

Recent advancements in deep learning technology have significantly boosted the restoration of degraded audio data, encompassing various forms of noise reduction and signal enhancement. This study delves into the use of deep learning methods for enhancing poor-quality music recordings, which are frequently encountered in archival collections and have become a growing area of interest. Given that a single transformation may fail to accommodate the diverse characteristics of music data, we introduce a music restoration network capable of adapting to distinct types of low-quality music recordings without specifically retraining the model. This architecture is built upon a generative adversarial network framework that allows for the simultaneous training of multiple domains using a shared latent space, which is dynamically determined based on the input mixture. We evaluate the proposed network using objective and subjective quality metrics on datasets compiled from the MuSCAN, DSD100, and DSD100 datasets. Compared to previous techniques and baseline GAN models, our approach demonstrates a significant improvement in subjective quality and non-inferiority in objective quality and perceived noise reduction measures.

This research proposes an end-to-end method to generate realistic throwing animations. The perception of realism in these animations depends on various factors, such as how realistic the initial posture, movement trajectory, and hand orientation look. Many existing studies focused on isolated aspects of this problem, such as hand posture. Our approach integrates multiple signal processing techniques to accurately predict the initial hand posture, and this prediction is incorporated into a style transfer network. The network, built on a VGG-16 architecture, takes an input image and a throwing style, and generates a detailed hand posture map as its output. The hand posture map is then combined with a traditional CNN model, and the combined system is used to generate novel throwing posture samples when training is complete. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated by evaluating hand posture accuracy and visually assessing the realism of the generated motions. The associated code can be found at: https://github.com/keunlee/throwing-synthesis.

Our research focuses on incorporating syntax-awareness into the attention mechanism of neural machine translation systems by directing attention to specific sentence sections according to linguistic structure. This novel approach is straightforward to implement and doesn't require significant computational resources. Our experiments with Chinese-to-English translations demonstrate that this addition yields more fluent and accurate results, including improved handling of sentences featuring branched or nested branching orders. A thorough evaluation of the underlying attention mechanism has been carried out to ensure its compatibility with our unique syntax-based solution.

We conducted a study using the Open Source PHOENIX code to simulate various snow lines in protoplanetary discs by modifying the water ice sublimation temperature to account for different binding energies. We calculated the snow lines for discs with different masses and distances from the star, using three distinct binding energies: 5 eV, 5.53 eV, and 6.03 eV. These values were chosen to represent different physical processes, such as a pure ice grain surface, a surface with oxygen exposure, and a surface completely sublimated from ice. As the binding energy increased, the snow lines moved closer to the star, with a larger mass of ice requiring a shorter orbital radius. A disc with a mass of 0.005 solar masses showed little variation in snow lines across all three scenarios, whereas a disc with a mass of 0.01 solar masses exhibited noticeable differences. Notably, snow lines within 20 AU of the star required a more extensive analysis than those at larger distances.

A novel statistical approach, the Universal Fit, enables accurate modeling of complex distributions derived from Transport Equations. This method's versatility allows it to accommodate various non-ideal effects by adjusting its parameters, thereby ensuring an exact match between theoretical and empirical distributions. By leveraging the advantages of both the Unified Power Distribution model and the Universal Fit framework, the UPD is developed to precisely describe a wide range of standardized distribution functions. The UPD model increases the model's reliability and scalability, thereby enhancing its potential for widespread applications. Additionally, the UPD model demonstrates a robust capacity for high-precision Resonance Analysis, thereby facilitating Resonance Location, and its scalability is theoretically compatible with modeling distributions of distributions.

We introduce a quantum machine learning approach known as quantum state learning, aimed at determining a unknown quantum state using an inductive algorithm. We begin by outlining suitable criteria for evaluating the performance of this algorithm, specifically focusing on the expectation values of arbitrary observables and the overlap with any given target state. We then derive a fundamental upper limit on the number of samples required to achieve a given level of performance, expressed in terms of the distance between classical correlation measurements. We exemplify this bound by analyzing sample complexity results for learning Gaussian states, pure states, and states constrained by few observables, and demonstrate how it surpasses or validates existing classical machine learning findings.

As geometrical optics principles become increasingly prevalent in computational physics and wave theory, determining the wave equation's solution and the leading term of the uniform asymptotic approximation has become essential. Improving the accuracy of the approximations for a wide range of geometrical parameters and observing phenomena at a large-scale factor significantly contributes to the validation and application of geometrical optics in various scenarios, specifically those involving potentials with support that spans the entire space or has varying complexity. Therefore, we provide enhanced formulas for the leading terms of the asymptotic approximation for non-compact support potentials, as well as potentials with support varying in complexity, while also addressing the behavior of observables in the context of the wave equation.

$\text{Transmutate}$ is a proposed method that employs an unconventional technique, where the classes in a dataset are literally transformed by 'changing their form.' Unlike traditional methods, which adjust the class boundaries, $\text{Transmutate}$ changes the class definitions by applying various operations such as shifting, rotating, scaling, etc. The class transformations in $\text{Transmutate}$ are inspired by authentic biological processes and are designed as 'transmutations.' We also introduce a novel concept called'mixture mutation,' which combines multiple classes in a dataset by blending their features. We demonstrate that the mixture mutation is an effective strategy to improve the classification accuracy, especially in datasets with uncertain class labels. Furthermore, $\text{Transmutate}$ introduces a unique strategy called 'evolutionary transmutation,' where a population of classes undergoes continuous and simultaneous transformation based on the fittest individuals, thus enabling the exploration-exploitation strategy effectively. We validate the efficacy of $\text{Transmutate}$ by performing extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and present the results in a concise manner.

Sample-efficient algorithms for multi-task linear regression share key drawbacks, including a lack of adaptability to related tasks and poor robustness against noisy data, as highlighted by standard regret bounds. To address these issues, we introduce a new model, \textit{MT-DRO}, which builds on the existing multi-task learning framework by incorporating unreliable data. We then establish a new regret bound, providing a sharper performance guarantee in more general scenarios and demonstrating superior task adaptability and robustness. To achieve this, we employ a conditional covariance approach to represent relationships between tasks and utilize this to develop highly efficient techniques for \textit{MT-DRO} problems. Specifically, our methods significantly outperform existing techniques by achieving an approximately linear reduction in parameters for many tasks, as shown through theoretical analysis and empirical verification.

Research in NLP for low-resource languages faces significant hurdles, largely stemming from a lack of required data, often complicating the use of advanced and research-based techniques. Two prominent methods, Post-Training Quantization and Knowledge Distillation, have shown potential to alleviate these challenges, although their effects vary across different languages. This study examines their effects while developing a standardized framework for comparing their outcomes in a multi-task, zero-shot setting, applying them to diverse tasks and languages.
